paragraphs: Collaborative learning aims to improve several parties’ models without requiring them to hand over their local data or models. One approach uses unlabeled public data as a shared basis for distillation. This paper studies how well that approach can work when many participants have statistically different data.

The authors analyze a representative distillation algorithm through kernel regression. They establish nearly minimax optimal performance for a nonparametric collaborative learning algorithm in a massively distributed, statistically heterogeneous setting. This means the theoretical performance is close to the relevant best possible worst-case benchmark, within the setting covered by their analysis.

The theory also guides a practical algorithm built with neural networks. Its central ingredient is feature kernel matching, which connects the theoretical assumptions to neural network implementations. Simulated regression tasks support the theoretical results and demonstrate practical feasibility. Together, the contributions give both a mathematical justification for this form of collaboration and a concrete way to translate that justification into a usable learning method.
neurips-2024-a-kernel-perspective-on-dis.tldr: A kernel analysis establishes near-optimal guarantees for distillation-based collaboration and motivates a practical neural network algorithm.

paragraphs: Safety testing for generative models often concentrates on deliberately malicious prompts. This paper examines a different concern: a user can submit a safe prompt and still receive an unsafe image. Such failures matter because protecting ordinary users requires examining unintended outputs as well as intentional attempts to bypass safeguards.

The authors introduce ART, an automatic red-teaming framework for text-to-image models. It combines a vision-language model with a large language model to connect unsafe generated images with the prompts that produced them. This connection helps the framework identify vulnerabilities more efficiently and makes systematic investigation possible beyond manually assembled examples.

Experiments reveal toxic outputs in the popular open-source models examined and support ART’s effectiveness, adaptability, and diversity. The authors also introduce three large-scale datasets for investigating these safety risks. The contribution is an evaluation framework and accompanying research material: it expands the kinds of failures that safety testing can uncover, including failures that affect people whose requests are benign.
neurips-2024-art-automatic-red-teaming-f.tldr: ART automatically investigates how benign text prompts can trigger unsafe image generation.

paragraphs: BeanCounter introduces a large public source of language-model training text drawn from business disclosures. It contains more than 159 billion tokens. The authors report that less than 0.1% appears in Common Crawl-based datasets and that it is an order of magnitude larger than datasets using similar sources, making it a substantial addition to existing training material.

The paper investigates whether this provenance offers advantages in data quality. The authors hypothesize that business disclosures are more factual and less toxic than web-based material. Their reported analysis finds that many demographic identities appear at similar rates but in significantly less toxic contexts. This supports the toxicity claim without establishing the broader factuality hypothesis as a demonstrated result.

To assess practical usefulness, the authors continue pretraining two language models on BeanCounter and compare them with their original versions. Toxic generation falls by 18–33%, while finance-domain performance improves. These findings support business disclosures as a sizable source of domain-specific training data that can improve the tested models’ behavior.
neurips-2024-beancounter-a-low-toxicity-.tldr: BeanCounter supplies business-disclosure text that reduced toxic generation and improved finance performance in two continually pretrained models.

paragraphs: Graph-based cognitive diagnosis learns representations of students, exercises, and concepts to support predictions about learning. Existing approaches combine these entities in a unified graph. The paper argues that this can weaken exercise and concept representations that should not depend on individual interactions, making the overall system less robust to noisy student interaction data.

DisenGCD separates learning across three graphs: a student-exercise-concept interaction graph, an exercise-concept relation graph, and a concept dependency graph. A meta multigraph module learns student representations through multiple adjustable propagation paths. These paths give student representations access to exercise information from shallower layers, addressing information that earlier approaches did not sufficiently exploit.

Graph attention modules learn the exercise and concept representations on their respective graphs, and a diagnostic function combines the three representation types for prediction. Experiments report better performance and robustness than state-of-the-art cognitive diagnosis methods. They also support the value of both separating the graphs and introducing the meta multigraph module, connecting the architectural choices to the reported improvements.
neurips-2024-disengcd-a-meta-multigraph-.tldr: DisenGCD separates student interactions, exercise relations, and concept dependencies to improve cognitive diagnosis performance and robustness.

paragraphs: Some graphs change in two intertwined ways: their connections evolve, and the text describing their nodes and edges changes too. Models working with these graphs must understand both relationships and language over time. DTGB addresses the shortage of benchmark datasets designed specifically for this combination.

The benchmark collects large-scale, evolving graphs from diverse domains, including changing text attributes and categories. It supplies standardized evaluation procedures for four tasks: predicting future links, retrieving destination nodes, classifying edges, and generating textual descriptions of relations. These tasks examine different ways that graph structure and text must inform one another.

The authors evaluate seven dynamic graph learning algorithms, variants that incorporate text through language-model embeddings, and six large language models. Their results reveal limitations in how existing models handle these graphs. The benchmark also supports analysis of how structural and textual changes should be incorporated together. Its contribution is a shared evaluation setting that makes this combined challenge explicit and allows methods to be compared across several practical uses.
neurips-2024-dtgb-a-comprehensive-benchm.tldr: DTGB benchmarks models on graphs whose connections and text change over time, exposing limitations in existing approaches.

paragraphs: Choosing a language model involves balancing answer quality, monetary cost, and response time. The best choice can also depend on the question and how it is prompted. This paper addresses the resulting decision problem when users need strong answers across many questions while staying within longer-term spending and latency constraints.

TREACLE learns a reinforcement learning policy that selects both the model and the prompting scheme. Its decisions use question embeddings, which reflect aspects of the query’s type or difficulty, and response history, which provides information about consistency among earlier answers. This makes selection sensitive to the current problem and available responses.

Evaluations on GSM8K, CSQA, and LLC, using various models and prompts, report cost savings of up to 85% relative to the tested baselines while maintaining high accuracy. That figure describes the largest reported saving, rather than a uniform reduction. The broader result is a way to adjust the accuracy-cost balance through a learned policy that accounts for the user’s constraints.
neurips-2024-efficient-contextual-llm-ca.tldr: TREACLE learns context-sensitive model and prompt choices, achieving up to 85% cost savings while maintaining high accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Surface electromyography measures electrical signals associated with muscle activity without invasive sensors. This paper explores wrist recordings as a source of typing information. Its motivation is that wearable muscle sensing could support subtle, information-rich computer input, with touch typing providing a concrete task for studying that possibility.

The authors introduce emg2qwerty, a dataset containing wrist signals recorded while people type on a QWERTY keyboard, together with ground-truth annotations and reproducible baselines. It includes 1,135 sessions from 108 users, totaling 346 hours. The recordings capture both a hierarchy of activity involving neurons and muscles and differences across users and recording sessions.

The baseline models adapt standard techniques from automatic speech recognition to predict key presses using only the muscle signals. The authors report strong baseline performance, establishing a practical starting point for subsequent research. The combination of annotated recordings, repeated sessions, and multiple users makes the dataset useful for investigating prediction from muscle activity and the challenge of transferring models across changing users or sessions.
neurips-2024-emg2qwerty-a-large-dataset-.tldr: emg2qwerty provides annotated wrist muscle recordings and reproducible models for predicting typed keys from muscle signals alone.

paragraphs: Building a shared representation for many modalities can require expensive training and large amounts of high-quality paired data. Ex-MCR addresses this problem by extending existing pretrained representation spaces. Its goal is to connect more modalities efficiently while retaining useful semantic relationships already learned within those spaces.

The paper contrasts this approach with C-MCR, which projects two non-overlapping modalities into a newly learned space. The authors argue that this projection loses substantial information from the original spaces. Ex-MCR instead extends one modality’s space into another, preserving semantic alignment in the space being extended. In the experiments, pretrained audio-text and 3D-image representations are connected to an existing vision-text space.

Without using paired data for this extension, Ex-MCR achieves performance comparable to advanced methods on audio-image-text and 3D-image-text tasks. It performs better when used alongside data-driven methods. The authors also observe alignment between extended modalities, such as audio and 3D. These results suggest that extending pretrained spaces can support connections beyond the specific modality relationships initially available.
neurips-2024-extending-multi-modal-contr.tldr: Ex-MCR connects additional modalities by extending pretrained representation spaces without paired data for the extension.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are often considered robust because their neurons resemble biological ones. This paper argues that much of the supporting work is experimental and that common design choices simplify relevant biological behavior. In particular, direct input encoding and fixed membrane-potential leakage may make robustness difficult to generalize across datasets and networks.

The authors develop a unified theoretical framework for constraints on spiking-network robustness. It suggests that changing input encoding and allowing the membrane-potential leak factor to evolve can improve robustness. These findings motivate FEEL-SNN, which combines frequency encoding with an evolutionary leak factor. The two components draw inspiration from selective visual attention and non-fixed leakage in biological neurons.

Experiments support the effectiveness of frequency encoding, the evolving leak factor, and their combination against different noises. The components also improve robustness when combined with established robustness-enhancement algorithms. The contribution therefore links a theoretical analysis to two concrete model changes, with empirical evidence for their usefulness both individually and together, rather than relying solely on biological resemblance as an explanation.
neurips-2024-feel-snn-robust-spiking-neu.tldr: FEEL-SNN combines frequency encoding and an evolving leak factor to improve spiking-network robustness, guided by a theoretical framework.

paragraphs: Numeric planning extends symbolic planning by allowing states to include numerical variables. Graphs are a natural fit for the symbolic part because they represent relationships among objects and can accommodate planning instances with different numbers of objects. This paper develops learning methods that also handle the numerical information.

The authors introduce a graph kernel for graphs containing both continuous and categorical attributes. This gives the model a way to compare planning instances while retaining both kinds of information. They also develop optimization methods for learning heuristic functions, which guide the process of solving numeric planning tasks. The intended models are data-efficient and interpretable.

In the reported experiments, the graph kernels are substantially more efficient and generalize better than graph neural networks for numeric planning. They also achieve competitive coverage relative to domain-independent numeric planners. These findings support graph kernels as a useful approach to this planning setting: a representation designed around mixed attributes can provide strong learning behavior while remaining competitive in its ability to solve tasks.
neurips-2024-graph-learning-for-numeric-.tldr: New graph kernels and heuristic-learning methods deliver efficient, generalizable numeric planning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Self-supervised representation learning can predict either internal representations or missing parts of the original input. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures, or JEPAs, follow the first approach. Masked autoencoders follow the second. A common motivation for JEPAs is that predicting representations may emphasize abstract information over fine details that are difficult to predict or uninformative.

This paper investigates the mechanism behind that intuition using deep linear models. It focuses on self-distillation, where an online encoder learns to predict a target encoder’s output, sometimes through an additional predictor. The simplified setting lets the authors examine the learning bias associated with prediction in representation space.

Even in a linear setting where the two approaches learn similar representations, the analysis finds a distinctive JEPA bias toward high-influence features, characterized by large regression coefficients. The result identifies a difference in what learning favors despite the similarity of the resulting representations. Because the analysis concerns simplified linear models, it offers a possible explanation for practical success rather than a universal account of nonlinear systems.
neurips-2024-how-jepa-avoids-noisy-featu.tldr: A deep linear analysis finds that JEPA-style prediction favors high-influence features, offering a possible explanation for its practical behavior.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the storage and computation required by a neural network, but deciding how far pruning can go calls for more than a successful heuristic. This paper seeks a fundamental threshold by placing a sparsity constraint directly on the loss function and analyzing the resulting geometry.

The authors use statistical dimension, a tool from convex geometry, to characterize a sharp phase transition associated with the pruning-ratio limit. Their analysis identifies weight magnitude and the sharpness of the loss landscape as two determining factors. In the abstract’s pruning-ratio terminology, flatter landscapes or smaller weight magnitudes generally correspond to a smaller ratio.

Computing the threshold raises its own challenge: accurately estimating the spectrum of a large Hessian matrix that is not positive. The paper develops efficient methods to address this calculation and uses the threshold to explain several existing pruning heuristics rigorously. Experiments show close agreement between the theoretical threshold and observed behavior, supporting the analysis as a way to understand pruning limits as well as practical algorithm choices.
neurips-2024-how-sparse-can-we-prune-a-d.tldr: A geometric analysis links pruning thresholds to weight magnitude and loss sharpness, with predictions closely matching experiments.

paragraphs: In a two-sided matching market, participants may need to learn their preferences through repeated matches. This paper studies that learning problem when one side consists of players and the other of arms. Performance is measured using regret relative to the player-optimal stable matching, so the analysis concerns learning while pursuing a particular stable outcome.

The authors propose an algorithm with regret bounded by O(N² log T / Δ² + K log T / Δ), where N is the number of players, K the number of arms, T the horizon, and Δ the minimum preference gap. Compared with the previous O(K log T / Δ²) guarantee, this removes K from the term with inverse-squared gap dependence.

The improvement is useful in common settings where there are substantially fewer players than arms, and experiments support this advantage. The paper also refines the analysis of centralized UCB: under the alpha-condition, its bound becomes O(N log T / Δ² + K log T / Δ). That stronger result depends on the stated condition and matches the displayed lower-bound dependence.
neurips-2024-improved-analysis-for-bandi.tldr: New regret guarantees improve bandit learning in matching markets with many arms, with a sharper UCB result under the alpha-condition.

paragraphs: Labels often have a hierarchy, yet representation learning commonly treats them as unrelated categories. This paper uses that available structure to shape learned features. Its motivation is that Euclidean distance can distort hierarchical semantic relationships, while hyperbolic geometry offers a setting suited to representing such relationships.

The proposed method, HypStructure, is a regularizer combining a hyperbolic tree-based representation loss with a centering loss. It can be added to a standard task loss, allowing the model to learn features informed by the label hierarchy alongside its main objective. The hierarchy therefore influences how examples are represented, rather than serving only as separate label information.

Experiments on several large-scale vision benchmarks show reduced distortion and improved generalization, particularly when representations have few dimensions. The authors also analyze eigenvalues to connect representation geometry with the improved out-of-distribution detection observed experimentally. The results support structured regularization as a way to preserve label relationships and improve the usefulness of learned features, with especially clear benefits in compact representation spaces.
neurips-2024-learning-structured-represe.tldr: HypStructure uses hyperbolic regularization to preserve label hierarchies and improve generalization, especially in low-dimensional representations.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph through differentiable optimization is complicated when several graphs fit the data equally well. Existing guarantees often require strong assumptions that make the true graph uniquely identifiable. This paper examines the broader situation of likelihoods with multiple global minimizers and addresses undesirable loss-function artifacts that optimizers can exploit.

The authors show that carefully regularizing the likelihood can identify the sparsest model in the Markov equivalence class even without an identifiable parametrization. They first develop the result for Gaussian models and then extend it to general models and likelihoods. Recovering the Markov equivalence class additionally relies on the stated faithfulness assumption.

Empirical results validate the theory using standard gradient-based optimizers, without approximations such as Gumbel-Softmax. The contribution clarifies what differentiable structure learning can recover when the data do not single out one parametrized graph. It also supplies a regularization-based route to that target, expanding the theoretical basis for learning structures under more general models and losses.
neurips-2024-markov-equivalence-and-cons.tldr: Careful likelihood regularization enables sparse graph recovery without unique identifiability, with equivalence-class recovery under faithfulness.

paragraphs: Point-cloud registration depends on finding accurate correspondences between two collections of 3D points. Coarse-to-fine approaches can struggle when initial coarse matches are unreliable or contain outliers. This paper improves correspondence filtering by checking whether a proposed match remains locally consistent across multiple feature scales.

The Hierarchical Sinkhorn Tree represents these checks as a pruned tree rooted at a superpoint. Its children come from nearest neighbors in a feature pyramid. The method traverses a pair of trees together, aggregates consistency measurements from corresponding nodes, and prunes locally dissimilar candidates. This turns multiscale consistency assessment into a structured traversal.

An overlap-aware Sinkhorn distance makes the comparison more selective by retaining only points most likely to overlap for local measurement and further exploration. This supports both efficient pruning and a more accurate description of the relevant neighborhood. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods on indoor and outdoor benchmarks. The findings support checking agreement across scales as a way to obtain more reliable correspondences for registration.
neurips-2024-multi-scale-consistency-for.tldr: Hierarchical Sinkhorn Trees filter unreliable 3D correspondences by checking local agreement across feature scales.

paragraphs: Image-text datasets often favor English because many evaluation benchmarks are English-centered. This paper asks whether discarding non-English examples also discards information useful for English vision tasks. Its premise is that multilingual sources capture both culturally specific concepts and different depictions of concepts shared across languages.

The authors translate multilingual image-text pairs from a raw web crawl into English and then filter the data again. This increases the share of examples originating in non-English sources while keeping the resulting text in English. They also measure differences between English-origin and non-English-origin data in both image space and translated text space.

Pretraining on the resulting dataset outperforms English-only or English-dominated alternatives on ImageNet, ImageNet distribution shifts, image-English-text retrieval, and the average across 38 DataComp tasks. On GeoDE, improvements occur in every region, with the largest gain in Africa. These findings show that multilingual provenance can benefit English-facing evaluations too, supporting data curation that considers the diversity of source material rather than language alone.
neurips-2024-multilingual-diversity-impr.tldr: Including translated non-English image-text data improves vision-language performance across English-facing and geographically diverse evaluations.

paragraphs: Neural networks are increasingly proposed for use inside databases, operating systems, and networked systems. Many such applications are safety critical, making it useful to formally check whether their networks satisfy required properties. This paper argues that these computer-systems applications have characteristics that existing verification tools overlook or support only to a limited extent.

NN4SysBench assembles a benchmark suite from impactful applications in this area. Its purpose is to expose verification challenges through concrete systems workloads. By bringing these applications into a common suite, the authors create a basis for examining the gap between what systems need and what neural-network verification currently handles.

The paper also provides a compatible version of the benchmark that existing verifiers can process while retaining approximately the same verification difficulties. This makes the benchmark usable for present tools as well as relevant to future development. The contribution is evaluation infrastructure: it connects formal verification research with the distinctive requirements of neural networks deployed as components of computer systems.
neurips-2024-nn4sysbench-characterizing-.tldr: NN4SysBench brings computer-systems applications into neural-network verification benchmarks, including a version compatible with existing tools.

paragraphs: This paper studies offline convex resource allocation under joint differential privacy with m hard constraints. The task is to produce useful allocations while satisfying a privacy requirement and controlling departures from the resource constraints. Its proposed algorithm, Noisy Dual Mirror Descent, coordinates allocations through privately computed shadow prices.

The algorithm relaxes the constraints to form a dual problem, applies noisy mirror descent to obtain prices, and uses those prices in the original allocation problem. Under weak duality, both the optimality gap and the violation per constraint are bounded at order √(m ln(1/δ))/ε. Under strong duality, exploiting the dual space’s geometry improves both bounds to order √ln(1/δ)/ε, up to logarithmic factors.

The authors also derive an Ω(m/ε) minimax lower bound for jointly private algorithms that output feasible allocations. They report matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors when ε ≥ max(1, 1/(nγ)), where nγ is the available resource level. Numerical studies support the algorithm’s effectiveness. The stronger guarantees therefore depend on explicit duality and parameter conditions.
neurips-2024-noisy-dual-mirror-descent-a.tldr: Noisy Dual Mirror Descent uses private shadow prices for resource allocation, with stronger near-optimal guarantees under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Models are often chosen before applying temperature scaling, ensembling, or stochastic weight averaging. This paper shows that such transformations can reverse the performance trends used to make the original choice. A model that looks worse before transformation may therefore be a better component of the final prediction system.

The authors call this phenomenon post-hoc reversal and find it especially prominent with high noise. For example, base models may overfit early even though ensembling and weight averaging favor longer training. Reversal can also remove the appearance of double descent and reduce disagreements between test loss and test error. Preliminary analysis suggests that suppressing the influence of mislabeled examples helps explain the behavior.

The proposed response is post-hoc selection: use performance after transformation to guide early stopping, checkpoint selection, and hyperparameter decisions. Experiments cover vision, language, tabular, and graph datasets. On one language-model instruction-tuning dataset, this approach produces more than a 1.5-fold MMLU improvement over naive selection. The practical lesson is to evaluate development choices in the form in which the model will ultimately be used.
neurips-2024-post-hoc-reversal-are-we-se.tldr: Post-training transformations can reverse model rankings, motivating selection based on the transformed system’s performance.

paragraphs: Language-model scaling usually considers model size and pretraining data. This paper studies a third dimension: how much information a retrieval-based model can access at inference time. The central question is whether expanding that external datastore offers a useful performance trade-off alongside increasing the model itself.

The authors construct MassiveDS, a 1.4-trillion-token datastore, and an efficient pipeline for studying datastore scaling. They vary datastore size, model size, and pretraining data to examine compute-optimal choices. They also analyze how retriever improvements, datastore quality filtering, and other design decisions affect the observed trends.

Across the studied range, larger datastores monotonically improve language modeling and several downstream tasks without obvious saturation. A smaller model with a large datastore outperforms a larger model without retrieval on knowledge-intensive tasks. Larger datastores also improve performance at a fixed training-compute budget. These results make datastore size a meaningful part of efficiency planning, while the reported lack of saturation describes the observed scaling range rather than an unlimited guarantee.
neurips-2024-scaling-retrieval-based-lan.tldr: Experiments with MassiveDS show that expanding retrieval data can improve language-model performance at a fixed training-compute budget.

paragraphs: Digital agents need demonstrations of how to complete tasks, but collecting them from people is expensive. Automatic exploration also requires substantial environment setup and may cover a limited range of scenarios. Synatra instead draws on indirect knowledge, such as tutorials written for people, and converts it into direct supervision for agents.

The paper studies types and sources of indirect knowledge, ways to represent the structure of demonstrations, and methods for performing the conversion. The authors generate 100,000 synthetic demonstrations and use them to fine-tune a 7-billion-parameter CodeLlama model. This turns existing instructional material into data that directly supports learning digital actions.

The resulting agent surpasses the comparably sized models evaluated on Mind2Web, MiniWoB++, and WebArena, and surpasses GPT-3.5 on Mind2Web and WebArena. The synthetic demonstrations cost $0.031 each, reported as 3% of human-demonstration cost. They can also outperform an equal number of human demonstrations collected from limited domains. That comparison highlights the potential value of coverage as well as collection cost.
neurips-2024-synatra-turning-indirect-kn.tldr: Synatra converts indirect instructional knowledge into inexpensive synthetic demonstrations that improve a digital agent on three web-task benchmarks.

paragraphs: Privacy mechanisms can impose communication costs when randomized outputs must be transmitted. This paper introduces Poisson private representation, or PPR, to compress and simulate local randomizers while ensuring local differential privacy. Its key aim is to reduce communication without changing the statistical behavior of the original mechanism.

PPR exactly preserves the joint distribution of the data and the randomizer’s output. Consequently, properties such as unbiasedness or Gaussianity are retained when the original mechanism has them. The construction also achieves a compressed size within a logarithmic gap of the theoretical lower bound, connecting exact preservation with a strong communication guarantee.

The authors apply PPR to distributed mean estimation and derive a new order-wise trade-off among communication, accuracy, central privacy, and local privacy. Experiments on that task consistently show a better communication-accuracy-central-privacy trade-off than the coordinate-subsampled Gaussian mechanism, while also providing local privacy. The result offers a way to compress private communication while preserving the original output distribution, rather than accepting statistical changes as part of compression.
neurips-2024-universal-exact-compression.tldr: PPR compresses private randomizers while exactly preserving their data-output distribution and improving reported distributed mean-estimation trade-offs.

paragraphs: Driving world models predict how scenes may evolve under different actions. Vista targets three difficulties in these models: transferring to unfamiliar environments, preserving important visual details, and responding to flexible action controls. The paper develops several components around these distinct requirements.

Two new training losses promote learning about moving objects and structural information for high-resolution prediction. A latent replacement method incorporates historical frames as prior information to support coherent predictions over longer horizons. Vista also accepts controls ranging from high-level commands and goal points to trajectories, angles, and speeds through an efficient learning strategy.

After large-scale training, experiments across multiple datasets show generalization to different scenarios. Vista outperforms the compared general-purpose video generator in more than 70% of comparisons and improves on the best-performing driving world model by 55% in FID and 27% in FVD. The authors also use Vista itself to construct a generalizable reward for evaluating real-world actions without accessing ground-truth actions. This extends its role from predicting outcomes to helping assess candidate actions.
neurips-2024-vista-a-generalizable-drivi.tldr: Vista improves driving-scene prediction and action control, and uses its own modeling capacity to evaluate actions without ground-truth actions.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning has been successful in vision and language, but its representation-learning mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This paper connects commonly used noise contrastive estimation losses to distribution alignment through entropic optimal transport. The connection provides a different mathematical view of how relationships among learned representations are organized.

Using that view, the authors develop a family of losses and multistep iterative variants for existing contrastive methods. These methods draw on more information from the distribution of latent representations when adjusting relationships within augmented sample sets. The approach therefore makes the alignment process more sensitive to the surrounding representation distribution.

The paper provides theoretical insights and experimental evidence supporting this generalized alignment framework. It also shows how optimal transport tools can yield unbalanced losses for noisy views and allow changes to alignment constraints to customize the representation space. The contribution is both explanatory and practical: it connects self-supervised learning methods through a shared formulation and offers tools for adapting their objectives to noise or relevant domain knowledge.
neurips-2024-your-contrastive-learning-p.tldr: Recasting contrastive learning as optimal-transport alignment yields new losses and tools for handling noise and shaping representations.
